new.title: Stroll under the glass roof of De Passage
new.desc: Opened in 1885, De Passage is the oldest shopping arcade still standing in the Netherlands. Its original arms run from the Spuistraat to the Buitenhof in neo-Renaissance style, and a third arm to the Hofweg was added in 1929 in a very different expressionist look.
new.tip: Look down as well as up: the marble floor was restored by Italian craftsmen. Chocolate maker Hop & Stork at number 82 is a good excuse to linger.

new.title: Step into the first public museum in the country
new.desc: Prince William V opened his picture gallery on the Buitenhof to the public in 1774, making it the first museum in the Netherlands anyone could visit. The walls are hung floor to ceiling in the crowded 18th-century manner, with works by Rubens, Jan Steen and Paulus Potter that belong to the Mauritshuis.
new.tip: The gallery is one long room, so half an hour is plenty. The entrance is shared with the Gevangenpoort next door.
new.q: Galerij Prins Willem V, Buitenhof, Den Haag

new.title: Have a drink at the oldest inn in Den Haag
new.desc: A tavern called 'In tgulde hoift' was already recorded on this spot in 1423. Pieter Post rebuilt it in 1660 and gave it the two golden heads on the facade; the present building is a faithful, slightly larger reconstruction that reopened in 1939.
new.tip: The big terrace on the Dagelijkse Groenmarkt is the place to sit on a sunny afternoon. Look up to find the golden heads before you order.
new.q: 't Goude Hooft, Dagelijkse Groenmarkt, Den Haag

new.title: Work through the beer list at De Paas
new.desc: De Paas has been the beer café of Den Haag since 1993, on the canal at Dunne Bierkade 16a. It pours 13 beers on tap and keeps around 190 more in bottles, alongside a serious shelf of jenever and whisky.
new.tip: It opens mid-afternoon, at 15:00 on weekdays and 14:00 at weekends. Ask for the staff's choice if the list is too long to read.
new.q: De Paas, Dunne Bierkade 16A, Den Haag

new.title: See the city from its canals with De Ooievaart
new.desc: Volunteer guides take open boats through the canals of Den Haag from April to October, telling the story of the court city along the way. The canal ring dates back to the 14th century and the bridges are low, which is why the boats are open.
new.tip: Boats leave from the visitors' café De Haagse Hop at Bierkade 19; be there 15 minutes early. Book ahead online on sunny weekends.
new.q: De Ooievaart rondvaarten, Bierkade, Den Haag

new.title: Walk through the whole country at Madurodam
new.desc: Since 1952 Madurodam has shown the landmarks of the Netherlands at a scale of 1:25. It was paid for by the parents of George Maduro, a law student from Curaçao who resisted the Nazi occupation and died in Dachau in 1945, as a memorial to their son.
new.tip: The net proceeds go to Dutch charities, so the ticket does some good. Go late in the afternoon, when school groups have left.

new.title: Look up at the painted ceiling of the Kurhaus
new.desc: The Kurhaus was built in 1884 and 1885 as a concert hall and seaside hotel, burned, and was rebuilt within two years. Kings and heads of state stayed here, and on 8 August 1964 the Rolling Stones played its great hall while crowds of fans laid siege to the building.
new.tip: It is still a hotel, and its largest room, the Kurzaal, has the painted ceiling. The best photo of the facade is from the beach side.

new.title: Find the lighthouse above the harbour
new.desc: The lighthouse of Scheveningen has stood at the end of the boulevard, near the harbour and the fish auction, since 1875. Designed by Quirinus Harder, it is 30 metres tall with a staircase of 159 steps inside.
new.tip: Come at dusk and watch the light start to turn, then walk down to the harbour for fish.

new.title: Eat the catch of the day at De Dagvisser
new.desc: De Dagvisser has served fish on the Dr. Lelykade, beside the harbour, since 1996. The kitchen buys at the fish auction every day, so the menu follows the season: sole, plaice, Zeeland mussels, oysters and lobster.
new.tip: Plaice, sole, oysters and mussels are seasonal and not always on. Parking on the quay is paid from 18:00.
new.q: De Dagvisser, Dr. Lelykade 26, Den Haag

new.title: Eat an ice cream on the boulevard at IJsCaffè Sì
new.desc: IJsCaffè Sì on the Strandweg makes its ice cream fresh every day with organic milk from farms in the region, without ready-made mixes. It also serves coffee, right on the Scheveningen promenade.
new.tip: Take your cone down the steps and eat it with your feet in the sand.

new.title: Visit Couperus and Mesdag at Oud Eik en Duinen
new.desc: Around 1247 Count Willem II had a chapel built here in memory of his father Floris IV; it was partly demolished in 1581. The cemetery around it holds writer Louis Couperus, painter Hendrik Willem Mesdag and post-war prime minister Willem Drees.
new.tip: The gates are open from sunrise to sunset. The entrance is on the Laan van Eik en Duinen.
new.q: Oud Eik en Duinen, Laan van Eik en Duinen 40, Den Haag

new.title: Sit under the dome at Museon-Omniversum
new.desc: The science museum Museon, founded in 1904 by a newspaper owner to support schools, merged in 2022 with the Omniversum dome theatre. Together they offer exhibitions on nature, history and technology plus planetarium shows and large-format films projected across a dome.
new.tip: It sits right beside the Kunstmuseum, so the two combine well on a wet day. Check which dome film is playing before you buy tickets.

new.title: Spend a beach day at quiet Kijkduin
new.desc: Kijkduin is the second, much smaller seaside resort of Den Haag, at the far western end of the city. Around 1900 it was not much smaller than Scheveningen, but about half of it was demolished for the Atlantikwall in the war and it stayed low-key afterwards.
new.tip: Walk south-west along the waterline towards the Zandmotor, the huge artificial sandbank off the coast.

new.title: Catch a summer show on the island in the Zuiderpark
new.desc: The Zuiderpark was laid out from 1923 as a job-creation project, following a plan by Berlage, and opened in 1936. On an island in the park is an open-air theatre built by unemployed workers and opened in 1941, which now seats about 2,500 for music, theatre and family shows in summer.
new.tip: Bring a cushion and a jumper for after sunset. On the way, look for the miniature steam trains that a local club has run in the park since 1975.

new.title: Try chai masala ice cream at Piet
new.desc: Piet Artisans of Flavour is the ice cream parlour of the Zeeheldenkwartier, on the Piet Heinstraat. The flavours go well beyond vanilla: think chai masala, sesame halva and Campari.
new.tip: There is a second branch on the Roggeveenstraat in the same neighbourhood if the queue here is long.

new.title: Drink coffee among the books on De Fred
new.desc: The Frederik Hendriklaan, 'De Fred' to locals, is the shopping street of the Statenkwartier. At number 217 is Paagman, a big bookshop with its own café inside.
new.tip: Pick up a book first, then order. The terraces along De Fred are the alternative when the sun is out.

new.title: Watch the deer beside Central Station
new.desc: The Koekamp was a hunting ground of the counts of Holland and is first mentioned in 1316. Today it is a small landscape park with ponds, laid out by Zocher in the 19th century, where red deer and fallow deer graze close to the station; an oak in the enclosure is almost 300 years old.
new.tip: It is a short walk from Den Haag Centraal, so it is perfect while waiting for a train. Do not feed the deer.

new.title: Walk the beech avenue of the Marlot estate
new.desc: Marlot takes its name from David van Marlot, a French-born nobleman who received the estate in 1640. The park is public: an old beech avenue runs along a canal, there are protected fruit walls from the late 17th century near the house, and it borders the Reigersbergen estate.
new.tip: Combine it with the Haagse Bos for a long green walk towards the centre. Look for the sandstone statue of Gerda and the reindeer from 1938.

new.title: Queue for a cone at Luciano in Bezuidenhout
new.desc: Luciano's ice cream is made by a certified master ice cream maker, and one of its Den Haag shops is on the Theresiastraat in Bezuidenhout. Allergy-friendly ice cream and cones are available too.
new.tip: The Theresiastraat is the neighbourhood's shopping street, so pair it with errands like the locals do.

new.title: Lunch in an old paint factory in the Binckhorst
new.desc: PuuRR aan de Binck is a restaurant in a paint factory from 1920, on the Fokkerhaven in the Binckhorst. It serves lunch and dinner, with sandwiches, salads, soup and vegan options at midday.
new.tip: On a warm day ask for a table on the waterside terrace. Brewery Kompaan is close by for afterwards.
new.q: PuuRR aan de Binck, Fokkerkade 18, Den Haag

new.title: See the Last Judgement at Museum De Lakenhal in Leiden
new.desc: The Lakenhal was built in 1640 by Arent van 's-Gravesande as the guild hall of Leiden's cloth merchants, and has been the city museum since 1874. Its treasures include the Last Judgement by Lucas van Leyden and early work by Rembrandt.
new.tip: The museum reopened in 2019 after a three-year renovation and is closed on Mondays.
new.q: Museum De Lakenhal, Oude Singel 32, Leiden

new.title: Order a pancake at Oudt Leyden
new.desc: The pancake house Oudt Leyden has been baking on the Steenstraat in Leiden since 1907, to its own recipe. Its guest list over the years includes Winston Churchill, Charles de Gaulle and members of the Dutch royal family.
new.tip: It is open every day from 11:30 to 21:30. The menu runs from traditional pancakes to more unusual ones.

new.title: Slide into the Tikibad at Duinrell
new.desc: Duinrell is an amusement park in Wassenaar, on a family estate that first opened to the public in 1935. It has more than 40 attractions, including three roller coasters, and the Tikibad water park with 21 slides.
new.tip: Check on the website how the Tikibad is ticketed before you go. Rick the Frog, the mascot, is hard to miss.
